DONETSK, Ukraine — Surface-to-air missiles pilfered from army bases. Defectors from Ukraine’s elite special forces. Russian fighters who slipped across a porous border.
These are some of the biggest problems facing Ukraine’s military in the rebellious east, and they were all on prominent display here in the unlikely setting of the
Donetsk Botanical Garden
, where the Vostok Battalion, the largest separatist militia in this city of one million people, has established a training camp.
“We are an international battalion,” said Aleksandr Khodakovsky, the rebel commander, who led the government’s Alfa special forces unit in the Donetsk region until he resigned after the February revolution in Kiev. Mr. Khodakovsky said that Russian citizens were among his fighters, but that the “overwhelming majority” of his force of more than 500 came from eastern Ukraine. He denied any link to Russia.
As the threat of a Russian invasion into eastern Ukraine has declined and appeals for annexation by rebel politicians have gone unanswered, the pace of fighting has picked up in eastern Ukraine with both the Kiev government and the separatists trying to seize momentum. Whether eastern Ukraine’s counterrevolution succeeds or crumbles depends increasingly on battle commanders like Mr. Khodakovsky and the fighters they command, whose resolve could extend the fighting here for weeks or even months to come.
In an interview, Mr. Khodakovsky said that he was largely autonomous, that he coordinated on some matters with other separatist military commanders and that he would even turn against the separatist government “if the interests of the politicians and the people diverge.”
But the main enemy remains the Kiev government, and until its military leaves the region, Mr. Khodakovsky said, his fighters will not lay down their arms.
“Everyone understands that this is a war between Russia and America, and we must be for one side or for the other,” Mr. Khodakovsky said in a confident, flowing monologue.
Across a well-tramped field, recruits were receiving instructions on how to use surface-to-air missiles, a 30-millimeter automatic grenade launcher, heavy machine guns and antitank weapons that Mr. Khodakovsky said he had taken from military bases in Ukraine.
The
offensive by the Ukrainian military
, which officials in Kiev have called an “antiterrorist operation,” continued on Tuesday, as armored personnel carriers and helicopters attacked rebel checkpoints near Slovyansk, a rebel stronghold. Arsen Avakov, the country’s acting police chief, said in a message on his Facebook page that the military had taken control of Semyonovka, a village to the south of Slovyansk.
The Ukrainian prosecutor, Oleh Makhnitsky, said on Tuesday that 181 people, including 59 Ukrainian service members, had died and an additional 293 people had been wounded since fighting began in the country’s east.
Since the Vostok Battalion appeared in early May and began leading the fight in Donetsk against the Ukrainian military, the militia’s composition has raised
questions about Russia’s role
in eastern Ukraine. When more than 40 of the militia’s fighters were killed in heavy fighting near the Donetsk airport last month, separatist leaders said that 33 were Russian citizens. Their bodies were sent in a refrigerated truck to the Russian border for repatriation.

In 1941, an Italian civil servant named Felice Benuzzi was captured by Allied forces and sent to a prisoner-of-war camp in East Africa. The camp faced Mount Kenya, 17,000 feet high, and Benuzzi found himself staring longingly at that larger, snow-blanketed world from the smallness of his own. Eventually he couldn’t help himself; he decided to climb the mountain.
It’s important to know two things about the adventure that followed, which Benuzzi chronicled in his book, “No Picnic on Mount Kenya.” First, Benuzzi did manage to escape the camp and climb to the summit of the mountain’s third-highest peak. (He and two other prisoners spent eight months clandestinely preparing: They made ice-climbing gear from barbed wire, and because they didn’t have a map of Mount Kenya, they consulted an illustration of it on a brand of canned food.) Second, when Benuzzi came back down, after 18 days on the mountain, he apparently felt so rejuvenated — as if he had absorbed enough beauty to sustain him — that he decided to sneak back into the camp and picked up his life again as a prisoner. The mountain was that large and impressive, that sublime.
This past October, the English photographer Simon Norfolk spent 18 days on Mount Kenya, camping in an old mountaineering hut at nearly 16,000 feet. Norfolk was there to document the gradual disappearance of one of the mountain’s many glaciers, the Lewis, which happens to be one of the most thoroughly surveyed tropical glaciers in the world. Its ice mass has been mapped periodically since 1934, and in recent decades, as the earth has warmed, scientists have reported on its catastrophic recession in their own quiet, peer-­reviewed way. In 1979, for example, glaciologists mapped the Lewis from an airplane and discovered ‘'drastic ice loss'’ since the last mapping four years earlier. In 1983, another survey found the same thing. There was similar bad news in a 1995 study (“climatic forcing of the glacier recession has accentuated in recent years”) and, likewise, a decade after that (“a drastic and progressive shrinkage.”) In 2010, scientists found that the Lewis had shrunk by 23 percent in just the previous six years. Worse still, a neighboring glacier — the Gregory — “no longer exists.”
Norfolk was disturbed that the death of something so large could be taking place so stealthily. It was happening over the course of so many human generations that it was essentially invisible to any one of them. He trekked to the Lewis Glacier because he had come up with a way to reveal its drama, to burn right through the problematic lag between glacial and human time scales. In these photographs, he has used fire to draw the former boundaries of the ice. Collaborating with a nonprofit organization called Project Pressure, he overlaid GPS coordinates onto that historical data about the Lewis Glacier’s size and shape. This allowed him to plot out the vanished edges of the glacier on the actual landscape. He then slowly walked those lines, in the middle of the night, with a makeshift torch: a length of shaggy white carpet rolled into a wick, soaked in gasoline, strapped to a garden rake.

It was so cold, and the air so thin, on the mountain that even walking with his fire-rake for 20 minutes exhausted Norfolk completely. He was like a man lost on an island, pacing and waving a flame for help. But his camera, set for an exposure of an hour or more, captured his movement as a solid line of fire: a burning scar.
Norfolk knew and loved the story of Benuzzi’s climb up Mount Kenya, but he got a very different feeling from the place. The mountain didn’t seem overwhelming or otherworldly now, but rather broken and vulnerable. As Norfolk worked, he could hear meltwater rushing down the glacier’s flanks. Standing next to that ice field, he says, was like standing next to “the exhausted remains of something that was once glorious.” He thought of nature documentaries, of scenes in which, say, a bull elephant is tranquilized by a researcher and crumples on the ground. “You can approach it now, because it’s safe,” Norfolk says. “But you feel its desperateness, as if it is opening one eye and looking back at you, saying, ‘What have you done to me?' ”
Most of us have probably never felt so indicted, so directly, by melting ice. Glaciers can feel like far away, abstract things — even in places like my home, San Francisco, that partly rely on them for water. Our glaciers, we’re told, are disappearing freakishly fast, but fast for a glacier can still be too slow for the human imagination to seize on. They’re like a lot of environmental problems that way: all these monstrous leaky faucets, on other floors of the house, that we know we ought to get around to fixing. The challenge, right now, is to find a way to make the slow deterioration of the world’s beauty feel as urgent and overpowering from afar as the beauty itself did to a man like Felice Benuzzi.
Jon Mooallem

SEATTLE —
Apple
and Samsung have been suing each other for years over patent disagreements. But
Microsoft
and Samsung took a different tack, signing a patent licensing deal in 2011 that has kept the peace between the two companies.
Until now. On Friday, Microsoft
filed a lawsuit
against Samsung,
accusing
the company of going back on the patent licensing deal the two signed three years ago.
In the lawsuit, Microsoft said that Samsung stopped making royalty payments to Microsoft last fall, as required by their
2011 agreement
, which related to Samsung’s use of Microsoft’s intellectual property in its Android smartphones and tablets. Samsung stopped making the payments, according to Microsoft, because it felt that Microsoft’s acquisition of
Nokia
‘s mobile business amounted to a breach of contract.
Microsoft denied that the Nokia deal, which was completed in April, violated the previous agreement. In a blog post, David Howard, Microsoft’s deputy general counsel and corporate vice president, suggested that the real reason Samsung decided to stop paying was that its smartphones sales have quadrupled since the two companies signed their agreement. While the terms of the deal are confidential, royalty payments by licensees like Samsung typically go up as sales increase.
Adam Yates, a spokesman for Samsung, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The heavily redacted lawsuit does not say how much money Microsoft believes it is owed by Samsung. Analysts have estimated that Microsoft receives billions of dollars a year in payments through licensing agreements with Android-device makers.
“Samsung predicted it would be successful, but no one imagined their Android smartphone sales would increase this much,” Mr. Howard wrote, adding that Microsoft has spent months trying to resolve its disagreement with Samsung.

To the Editor:
Re “
A View From Gitmo
,” by Ramzi Kassem (Sunday Review, June 8):
How many of the 149 prisoners at Guantánamo Bay are incarcerated lawlessly? Here’s our tally:
Seventy-eight have been cleared for release by the Obama administration as posing no threat. But the administration finds it politically inconvenient to release them.
The government classifies 38 as too dangerous to release but unable to be prosecuted. It is unwilling to take its case to a court or even one of its own self-created military commissions.
Twenty-three have been “referred for prosecution,” but the government’s chief military commissions prosecutor has said that most of them will not in fact be prosecuted in any forum. In any event, they have been held far longer than is consistent with any concept of a speedy trial.
There are seven active prosecutions before military commissions. The use of these tribunals in “the war on terror” is legally untenable, and there are excellent reasons to believe that any convictions will be nullified by the courts.
Three prisoners have been convicted by military commissions. One of those outcomes has been overturned in court, and the government is in the last stages of an unpromising appeal. As to the other two, it is a fair prediction that the government will either avoid judicial scrutiny by transferring the prisoners or giving them irresistible plea deals, or those convictions will be voided by the courts as well.
There is no reckoning by which this tally is consistent with the rule of law.
ERIC M. FREEDMAN
BRIAN E. FOSTER
Hempstead, N.Y., June 8, 2014
The writers, a constitutional law professor at Hofstra and a lawyer in private practice, respectively, are engaged in the representation of numerous detainees at Guantánamo Bay.

A yawning victory margin for a Democratic governor. An incumbent who seemed intent to run out the clock, playing down the importance of debates. And a liberal base that felt shortchanged once the votes were counted, upbraiding the man atop the New York State ballot for not doing more.
Twenty-eight years after Gov.
Mario M. Cuomo
’s sweeping re-election victory, his son, Gov.
Andrew M. Cuomo
, has reprised the feat on several fronts, both substantive and superficial.
Both Cuomos focused zealously, long before Election Day, on securing landslide victories, stoking chatter about possible national ambitions. Both bested a Republican Westchester County executive by double digits — Rob Astorino in 2014, Andrew P. O’Rourke in 1986 — without ever breaking much of a sweat on the campaign trail. And both angered many on the left who said the governors had not done enough to help fellow Democrats.
“Certainly, Cuomo had the opportunity, if he felt like it, to work for a lot of other people — but he didn’t,” said Maurice Carroll, assistant director of the Quinnipiac University Poll and a longtime political writer. “He ran to get re-elected, which he did, very successfully.”
Mr. Carroll was asked which Cuomo he was referring to. “Either of them,” he said.
After the younger Cuomo’s triumph on Tuesday, perhaps the most stinging rebukes came from the
Working Families Party
, the liberal group that endorsed the governor this year, over the objections of many of its members, after he agreed to pursue a long list of its goals.
The deal, brokered by Mayor Bill de Blasio of New York, called on Mr. Cuomo to help elevate Democrats to a majority in the State Senate. But during the campaign, the governor at times
appeared indifferent
to the outcome of elections in the Legislature. He also promoted a new party, the Women’s Equality Party, that rivaled the Working Families Party.
Bill Lipton, state director of the Working Families Party, said the governor “squandered millions on a fake party, and left millions more in his campaign account as New York Democrats in the Legislature and in Congress withered on the vine.”
National Democrats also had choice words. Representative
Steve Israel
of Long Island, the chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said his group had spoken several months ago with the governor’s staff about “helping to organize and coordinate a campaign.”
Mr. Israel said he “didn’t see the fruition” of those conversations.
Aides to Mr. Cuomo have defended his efforts on behalf of Democrats, noting that the state
Democratic Party
, which he controls, spent more than $1 million helping candidates for State Senate. (The state
Democratic Party
reported spending nearly $17 million this year through late October, a majority of which went to Mr. Cuomo.)
A spokesman, Matt Wing, said the governor endorsed “nearly every candidate” and attended numerous events with candidates on the “women’s equality agenda, which was the best tool we had to push back the Republican tide.”

of slaughter in a rural church. She recently

A smell, a soft breeze, a shadow dancing on a wall is often all I need. I remember the utter stillness of Nyarubuye and the way the dust smoked up around my shoes. To the Editor:
“
Don’t Teach Math, Coach It
,” by Jordan Ellenberg (Op-Ed, July 25), disregards what American education needs today. Mr. Ellenberg wants to make math “fun” for our young students. But our children have too much fun, and not enough teaching.
Here I can cite from my own career. This has been a rewarding vocation as an inventor primarily in transfer of heat to fluids. In my college work, I found courses in heat transfer uninteresting. I skipped them. Someone then found it amusing to direct my life work toward heat transfer. Since I had been taught a firm grounding in mathematics, it was easy to learn the subject on my own.
This teaching started in the first grade. Then I learned simple arithmetic. It was no fun. It continued to lack merriment throughout my studies in advanced calculus in college. I learned the subject well enough to obtain more than a hundred patents. There was no fun in what math I used. Satisfaction, yes, was present in the work.
The same gratification existed in using woodworking tools with skill in my hobby. Skin cuts endured while I obtained that skill detracted from the learning fun.
We emphasize fun in our teaching to the level that learning is absent.
KEN COWANS
Fullerton, Calif., July 25, 2014

BEIRUT, Lebanon — An international team sent to investigate
allegations that chlorine gas had been used as a weapon
in Syria’s civil war came under attack on Tuesday, forcing it to abort its mission to reach a village where numerous such attacks have been reported.
In a statement, the team from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, which is collaborating with the United Nations in overseeing Syria’s promise to abandon chemical weapons, said all of its investigators were safe and had returned to their base.
The Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons has been working since last year to help Syria dispose of its chemical weapons under an agreement reached to avert threatened American strikes, after Aug. 21 chemical attacks that the Americans blamed on Syrian forces killed hundreds of people near Damascus, the Syrian capital.
Recently, however, antigovernment activists have accused the government of
hitting rebel areas with chlorine gas
, which is not normally considered a chemical weapon, to inflict misery on the rebels and their civilian backers.
The fact-finding mission was trying to reach Kfar Zeita, a village where a number of such attacks have been reported, when its vehicle was struck on Tuesday.
The Syrian government and the rebels blamed each other for the attack.
The government said in a statement that before the convoy of four United Nations vehicles reached their destination, one of them was hit with an explosive charge, forcing the passengers to transfer to the other three vehicles. Only one of those managed to leave the area, the statement said, adding that six investigators and five Syrian drivers had been kidnapped by “terrorist groups,” as it describes the rebels.
Antigovernment activists in the area, however, said the government had staged the attack to prevent investigators from reaching the site and posted videos online
showing the investigators talking with rebels
about which road they should use. It was unclear whether the video was taken before or after the attack.

The Bolshoi Ballet of Moscow is emerging from the worst ballet scandal in recent history. Its artistic director, Sergei Filin, is still
undergoing operations
to restore his eyesight after the severe injuries he suffered in a shocking acid attack in January 2013. Since he became director in 2011, the list of Bolshoi dancers has changed considerably: New stars have been imported, while existing ones have left in a wide range of circumstances — some for other companies (claiming the Bolshoi repertory held them back) and others as part of the fallout from the scandal.
I recently spent a week in Moscow watching five of its performances ahead of the company’s appearances in
Washington
in May and in
New York
in July. The Bolshoi is so vast and complex an organization that even experienced observers find it hard to grasp its true state of health. Even while I was there, I could scarcely reconcile the fresh, energetic troupe that fielded three impressive casts in Pierre Lacotte’s “
Marco Spada
” with the stale one that churned out the two dullest “Giselles” of my experience.
Why does the Bolshoi matter outside Moscow? Many seasoned balletgoers ultimately prefer the styles of certain Western companies or that of the Mariinsky Ballet of St. Petersburg. Yet your knowledge of ballet is incomplete until you’ve witnessed how the Bolshoi can seem the most red-blooded, exuberant and viscerally stirring of ballet companies. As the singing of the great Russian bass
Feodor Chaliapin
did a century ago, the best Bolshoi dancing has expressed the soul of a populace.
Today’s Bolshoi teeters in several different directions. For some, both inside and outside the institution, the company’s brightest flame and its truest hope remains
Yuri Grigorovich
— who, now 87 but still active as a choreographer, was the company’s artistic director from 1964 to ’95, and who, with his 1968 version of
“Spartacus,”
gave it one of its most celebrated, enduring and artistically crude hits. In Moscow, one dancegoer described him as “not a good man but a great one.”
I am among those who feel he did more damage than good to the Bolshoi, and wish the company would move more firmly out of his shadow. I regard with considerable misgiving the number of his productions, some recent, in the company’s current repertory.
In 2003, the Bolshoi began opening a series of new doors. That was when the choreographer Alexei Ratmansky created for the Bolshoi
“The Bright Stream,”
a full-length comic hit that released long-dormant aspects of Russian dance-acting skill. In 2004, he was made the company’s artistic director, in which capacity he linked the Bolshoi to its 19th-century history, its Soviet history and the new world of Western choreography. He made ballets of a subtlety and quality of mind unseen in Russia for 80 years. He also championed the young dancers Natalia Osipova and Ivan Vasiliev, who became international
superstars in 2007
during a Bolshoi season in London. In them, the old larger-higher-bolder Bolshoi characteristics were more in evidence than they’d been for many years.
Continue reading the main story
In 2008, Mr. Ratmansky moved to the West (he is American Ballet Theater’s artist in residence). But he returned to Moscow to make the full-length
“Lost Illusions” (2011)
, and he is an important link to
Mr. Filin
, who had been one of his lead Bolshoi dancers and who became the Bolshoi’s director in 2011. Today’s Bolshoi, however, is no longer led by a choreographer’s vision; and even Mr. Ratmansky was not there long enough to convince the old guard that his vision was the right one.
Mr. Filin continued the Ratmansky policy of openness to multiple historical traditions and to a wide range of Western choreographers dead and alive. His taste in dancers has been especially striking. When the highly distinctive
Olga Smirnova,
St. Petersburg born and bred, graduated from Vaganova Ballet Academy in 2011, she was invited to enter both the Mariinsky and Bolshoi Ballets at soloist level; she chose the Bolshoi because Mr. Filin’s offer was the more artistically rewarding.
The experienced ballerina
Evgenia Obraztsova
left the Mariinsky in 2012 to join the Bolshoi. More exceptionally yet, Mr. Filin in 2011 invited
David Hallberg,
the most princely male dancer ever produced by the United States, to become a Bolshoi dancer. Within weeks of Mr. Hallberg’s doing so, a live broadcast of “The Sleeping Beauty” showed how he — currently unmatched for pure classical style in this ballet — was now dancing with new spaciousness and sweep.
Who can yet tell how much Mr. Filin’s enterprise has been strengthened or weakened by the acid affair? Some of the company’s dissidents have left, but the scandal’s consequences strongly suggest that the larger artistic climate in Russia is also laden with corruption. The bizarre superstar dancer
Nikolai Tsiskaridze
— who behaved atrociously before and
after the acid scandal
— was forced out of the Bolshoi, only to be promptly consoled with the directorship of the Vaganova, Russia’s most prestigious center of academic ballet training. Senior
figures in Russian ballet
have expressed concern about this appointment.
The list of stars the company could bring to New York is a long one. I’ve yet to see in person the male principals Vladislav Lantratov and
Ruslan Skvortsov
, who have made very fine impressions in live high-definition broadcasts. Mr. Lantratov is young — only five years after joining the company, he created the lead role of Lucien in
“Lost Illusions,”
in which his acting, on screen, showed all the subtlety that Mr. Ratmansky has released in younger dancers. Ekaterina Shipulina, Anastasia Stashkevich, Maria Vinogradova, Igor Tsvirko and Artem Ovcharenko were among those I admired in Moscow, and of whom I hope to see more.
We won’t see Ms. Osipova, who quit the Bolshoi in 2011 and now dances with the Royal Ballet of London and the Mikhailovsky Ballet of St. Petersburg. Will we see Mr. Vasiliev, who left with her and who dances just one role with Ballet Theater this spring? He has been taking class again with his alma mater in Moscow.
Larger than stars, though, is the problematic choice of repertory. Two of the three productions to be seen in New York,
“Swan Lake”
and “Spartacus,” are by Mr. Grigorovich, as is the “Giselle” that will be danced in Washington. New York will also see that old Bolshoi war horse
“Don Quixote,”
in its 1999 production by Alexei Fadeyechev. Why is New York being fed nothing but this old pre-Ratmansky face of the Bolshoi?
Continue reading the main story
By contrast, in 2012 the company brought its beautiful 2009 production of the 1884
“Coppélia”
to
Washington
, last summer it showed its 2012 staging of George Balanchine’s 1967 classic
“Jewels” in London
and this January it danced
“Lost Illusions” in Paris
. The programming of these 2014 American dates does not suggest a company that is proud of its latest wares; it does suggest a troupe whose pro-Grigorovich faction is currently uppermost.

The ways in which Mr. Grigorovich reshaped the Bolshoi were extensive and drastic. The company’s first Western appearances occurred in 1956 in London. The Stanislavskian realism, the folk vigor and the fervor of Bolshoi style were at once apparent from Leonid Lavrovsky’s
“Romeo and Juliet”
and other productions. The British, who prided themselves on vivid acting, were startled to see how characters in
“Giselle”
lifted goblets; though no actual fluid was in them, the performers made the wine’s weight apparent. The national dances in “Swan Lake” (the performers, wearing heeled shoes, were sensational in their through-the-body verve) were a knockout for all observers.
But when Mr. Grigorovich produced his extensively revised “Swan Lake” in 1969, those dances had become restyled, with the female national dancers now
on point
. By the mid-1970s, many noticed that there was nothing special about the character acting in “Giselle.” By 1976, when I watched a live TV transmission of a Bolshoi “Romeo” from Moscow, there was little resemblance left to the Lavrovsky version; and in 1979 Mr. Grigorovich replaced it with his own, where communicative acting was replaced by unspecific dance waffle (albeit intensely delivered). In his 1986 “Giselle,” the heroine was more ballerina than peasant. A complete U-turn in Soviet ballet aesthetics had been achieved.
Until the late 1980s, nonetheless, the Grigorovich company kept exhibiting a potent supply of the world’s most colorful and distinguished performers. Certain Bolshoi feats stayed stunning — not least, acrobatic lifts. A man could run across the stage, carrying a woman overhead with just one hand. A lifted woman could arch in the air as if only his hands were preventing her from returning to the ether. The power, suppleness and ardor of Bolshoi spines often amazed. Thrilling too was the way men would hurl the front leg in jumps, like a javelin.
In recent seasons at Ballet Theater, audiences have seen how Ms. Osipova and Mr. Vasiliev have jumped higher and eaten up more space than any other dancers today. Their style was quintessential Bolshoi; like no other dancers of our century, they made the stage of the Metropolitan Opera House look small. (The width of that stage is 54 feet, but the
Bolshoi’s home stage
is over 68 feet.)
In establishing those two whiz kids, the Bolshoi seemed to recapture much of its own essence: The way they seemed not just to dance but to make huge claims on life itself, was just why the company had been a sensation in the West from the mid-1950s to the late ’80s. And yet the modern Bolshoi could not keep them.
Until Mr. Ratmansky, a drawback of Bolshoi repertory for Western dancegoers was the choreographic thinness of all its Soviet-era repertory; and a high proportion of the Bolshoi genius was all about transcending trash. No company has been more associated with the full-length “Don Quixote”; although this is a largely terrible collection of clichés, these Russians made it life-enhancing fun. Thinner, more serious and more ludicrous was Mr. Grigorovich’s “Spartacus”; and yet I’m among those who have cheered heartily for some of the superlative performances it has elicited.
But such ballets belong to a bygone Bolshoi. Mr. Grigorovich is still creating works, but has had no important success for decades. And although Ms. Osipova and Mr. Vasiliev were in some ways stylistic throwbacks, their careers have shown that they long for fresh challenges. So evidently do many in the home troupe, which, like other Russian companies, dances a thoroughly international repertory. New York, which will get the kind of productions the Bolshoi was dancing in the Soviet era, will see only a limited part of the picture. Back home in Moscow, the fight for the Bolshoi’s soul will continue.

BERLIN — The German government has approved the sale of the utility RWE’s oil and natural gas subsidiary, RWE Dea, to a team of Russian investors, the company confirmed on Friday.
The decision comes despite the tensions between the
European Union
and Russia over the crisis in Ukraine.
RWE agreed in March
to sell Dea to the LetterOne Group, an investment vehicle based in Luxembourg and owned by the Russian billionaires Mikhail Fridman and German Khan for 5.1 billion euros, or roughly $7 billion.
“With this decision, we have taken another important step in the sales process,”  Brigitte Lambertz, a spokeswoman for RWE, said.
The company is struggling to adjust to losses brought about by Germany’s decision to exit nuclear power and increase its reliance on renewable energy sources. It had sought for months to divest its energy assets, before reaching the agreement with Mr. Fridman. One of Russia’s wealthiest businessmen, he also heads the Alfa Group, which has investments in banking and telecommunications. Mr. Khan is his longtime business partner.
LetterOne’s base in the European Union was a decisive factor in the deal, said Stefan Kapferer, a deputy German economy minister, Reuters reported. Berlin decided the sale did not pose any danger to Germany’s energy supply, Mr. Kapferer said.
The German government decision was the biggest hurdle to the deal’s approval, but several other countries must also sign off on it. RWE declined to identify those countries, but the subsidiary also has production or stakes in locations in Norway, the British North Sea, Denmark and Egypt.

A Swedish tobacco company’s
petition to soften the warning labels
on its smokeless chewing tobacco will force the Food and Drug Administration to decide whether a product that is less harmful than smoking tobacco should be allowed to market itself as a safer option.
The same question of whether to allow a marketing distinction between levels of harm in tobacco-based products has been raised by electronic cigarettes.
The application by the seller of snus (pronounced “snoose”) to put softer “modified risk” warnings on its product is the first to receive full consideration by the F.D.A. under a 2009 law that allows alternative labels. The agency hopes to rule by June.
The issue is whether modified warnings would encourage tobacco use in somewhat less toxic forms and if such a result would be better for public health. For now, there’s no strong evidence that a modified warning would help many individual users or benefit the population as a whole. Unless there is such evidence, a softer label might only lure more people into the nicotine market.
Currently, warning labels on all smokeless tobacco products, using wording required by law, say that the products can cause mouth cancer, gum disease and tooth loss and are not a safe alternative to cigarettes. Swedish Match, the seller, wants to eliminate these specific disease warnings, and modify the label to say that “No tobacco product is safe, but this product presents substantially lower risks to health than cigarettes.”
The company says greater use of snus in Sweden since the 1970s has contributed significantly to reduced smoking rates and lower rates of tobacco-related diseases such as lung and oral cancer.
But the causation is debatable, since Sweden was simultaneously cracking down on smoking through various bans, restrictions and public health campaigns. In a
report
in The Times on Sunday, Matt Richtel and David Jolly examined the company’s F.D.A. petition and cited independent experts who found that snus is not nearly as lethal as cigarettes but that it is not risk-free either, especially for users who also smoke.
The danger is that snus might lead some nonsmokers and former smokers to take up the tobacco habit, and perhaps progress on to cigarette smoking, when abstention would be the safest approach.
The Swedish Match process for making snus results in lower levels of carcinogens and toxic substances than are found in other smokeless tobacco products, according to the World Health Organization. If the F.D.A. approves any modification in the warnings, it will be for a limited time period, to allow monitoring of how well it works, and it will apply only to certain snus products and not other kinds of smokeless tobacco.

Each of the world’s major film festivals has a special flavor and purpose. Some arrange the crown jewels of world cinema in a fancy European setting. Others line up horses for the Oscar race or parade indie darlings through the snow. The
New York Film Festival
, whose 52nd edition begins on Friday, takes its name and inspiration from the world capital of talk, and its clear and consistent ambition has been to start as many arguments as possible.
So let’s not waste any more time. The opening film is “Gone Girl,” David Fincher’s adaptation of the best-selling novel by Gillian Flynn, and you can find a smart and spoiler-avoidant conversation starter
in a review by Manohla Dargis
. Mr. Fincher, whose
“The Social Network”
opened the festival in 2010, is the kind of filmmaker that critics (including those on the festival’s selection committee) prize: an artist working with big budgets in popular genres whose movies are stamped with personal vision and executed with impeccable technique.
“Gone Girl” will receive a lot of attention, and bring a spritz of Hollywood glamour to Lincoln Center and the opening-night party. (Ben Affleck is in it! So are Rosamund Pike, Tyler Perry and Neil Patrick Harris.) But it serves less as a distraction than as a gateway, opening up a room full of beauties and curiosities, along with some puzzles.
You can think of a film festival as a collection of stories and styles. This one includes the austerity of Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne’s
“Two Days, One Night,”
with Marion Cotillard as a Belgian factory worker, and the abrasiveness of Alex Ross Perry’s
“Listen Up Philip,”
with Jason Schwartzman as a New York novelist. But a festival is also, for its audience, a succession of moods and atmospheres. We begin with the chilly suspense of “Gone Girl” and end with the wild kineticism of “Birdman or the Unexpected Virtue of Ignorance,” Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s backstage comic fantasy, which closes the festivities on Oct. 12.
Continue reading the main story
In between is a main slate of 29 more films (including the centerpiece, Paul Thomas Anderson’s
“Inherent Vice”
; a program of experimental films — now called
“Projections,”
instead of
“Views From the Avant-Garde”); and a robust
sidebar of documentaries
. Among these are
“The Look of Silence,”
Joshua Oppenheimer’s follow-up to
“The Act of Killing”
;
“Stray Dog,”
Debra Granik’s portrait of a middle-aged Missouri motorcyclist; and “Seymour: An Introduction,” Ethan Hawke’s examination of the life and philosophy of an octogenarian New York piano teacher.
Quite a lot to talk about, in other words. But, for now, let’s focus on the
main slate
over the next few days. Here are brief critical notes on the first nine features that follow “Gone Girl.”
MISUNDERSTOOD
Asia Argento’s latest feature as director is, like her last one (
“The Heart Is Deceitful Above All Things”
), the story of a suffering child. Based loosely on her own experiences, it follows a young girl named Aria (the wide-eyed and wonderful Giulia Salerno), as she bounces between the households of her vain, shallow movie star father and her volatile, narcissistic musician mother. This is perhaps not the most formally rigorous movie in the festival, but its messiness is heartfelt, affecting and occasionally glorious.

LA SAPIENZA
This is probably the most formally rigorous movie in the festival, an intellectual drama as stately and harmonious as the Baroque architecture that is one of its main themes and visual resources. Eugène Green, an American who has worked in Europe for most of his career (and who makes an amusing park bench cameo here), offers a series of decorous meditations in picturesque settings, but the serenity of the actors — who speak in perfect paragraphs of French and Italian and never interrupt one another — masks a rich and complicated emotional subtext. What looks like a treatise on aesthetics turns out, on closer inspection, to be a piercing study of romantic disappointment and forbidden passion.
’71
Jack O’Connell, who was remarkable as a young prisoner in David Mackenzie’s “
Starred Up
,” plays a green British soldier, patrolling Belfast in the worst days of the Troubles, in Yann Demange’s debut feature. The action takes place over the course of a single, stressful night during which all the city’s factions converge in a violent nexus of score settling and double-crossing, as Mr. Demange proves himself an agile juggler of suspense and political implication.
MAPS TO THE STARS
David Cronenberg brings his own brand of formal rigor to Bruce Wagner’s unholy mess of a screenplay, a survey of Hollywood depravity wrapped around a ghoulish family tragedy. Julianne Moore is terrifying and hilarious as an actress with career issues and mommy issues, and Evan Bird is spookily poised as a sociopathic child actor with issues of his own.
GOODBYE TO LANGUAGE
Godard in 3-D! What more is there to say? The title notwithstanding, the master’s latest work — mischievous, mournful and maddeningly elusive — is fairly chatty. It is also packed with arresting images, deep thoughts, gratuitous nudity and enough cute dog footage to make Mr. Godard a YouTube sensation.
WHIPLASH
Miles Teller is an ambitious jazz drummer at a prestigious, pressure cooker music school, where J. K. Simmons is the resident sadistic genius. Directed by Damien Chazelle, this film, which follows a fairly conventional sports movie template, is propelled by a potent musical score and a serious, ethically complex set of ideas about art, discipline and the pursuit of greatness.
TWO SHOTS FIRED
The latest film from the Argentine director Martín Rejtman is, for me, the sleeper of the festival, though its oblique narrative style and deadpan tone may be more baffling than beguiling for some viewers. In the first scenes, after a night out dancing, a teenager (Rafael Federman) wakes up, mows the lawn, finds a gun and shoots himself twice. He survives, and the rest of the movie explores the consequences, for himself, his brother, their mother and a handful of other people. Or maybe the surprising lack of consequences, since Mr. Rejtman’s achievement is to obliterate any conventional distinction between the trivial and the profound. He’s one of the best inaction directors around.
THE BLUE ROOM
Adapting and updating a novel by Georges Simenon, Mathieu Amalric takes a simple, economical tale of adultery and murder and turns it into a teasing, somber, erotic adventure. Instead of explanations, it supplies implications and whispers, and Mr. Amalric, uncharacteristically quiet, is brilliant as a man unable to comprehend or master the force of his desire.
HILL OF FREEDOM
Hong Sang-soo is another master of inaction cinema. His great subject is emotional passivity, particularly as practiced by South Korean heterosexual men. This time his protagonist is Japanese: a man named Mori, looking for love in a Korean city, though he may not be looking that hard. An ingenious conceit allows Mr. Hong to tell his purposefully banal story out of order, which gives it both humor and a wispy poignancy.

The American work force has been growing polarized for decades. On one end, there are highly skilled jobs like writing software or performing surgery, and on the other are service jobs like child care and cutting hair. The jobs in the middle, meanwhile, such as factory work, sales and bookkeeping, are shrinking — one of the reasons for the economy’s slow climb out of the recession.
Where did those jobs go? Part of the answer lies in Silicon Valley. It is no coincidence that many of those jobs entail the same repetitive tasks that computers, robots and other machines are uniquely suited to perform, from
robots loading conveyor belts
in factories to Kayak.com selling airline tickets.
A
new working paper
from the National Bureau of Economic Research shows how the recession
accelerated the displacement
of these midwage jobs. As technology now encroaches on jobs that people assumed would always belong to humans, it is useful to consider those most affected by the job displacement so far: the young, the less educated and men.
A lot of economic research has focused on the polarization of jobs, notably by
David Autor
of M.I.T. He
differentiates between
routine tasks that follow well-defined procedures — the kind of midwage jobs that computers have become so good at — and nonroutine ones that require flexibility, problem-solving and human interaction.
The new study, which analyzed data from the Current Population Survey from 1976 to 2012, illustrates that the recession had a disproportionately large effect on routine jobs, and greatly sped up their loss. That is probably because even if a new technology is cheaper and more efficient than a human laborer, bosses are unlikely to fire employees and replace them with computers when times are good. The recession, however, gave them a motive. And the people who lost those jobs are generally unable to find new ones, said
Henry E. Siu
, an associate professor at the University of British Columbia and an author of the study.
Young people and those with only a high school diploma are much more likely to be unemployed and replaced by a machine, he said. And to the authors’ surprise,
men are more vulnerable
than women.
“When you look at data, women who would otherwise be finding middle-paying routine jobs tend to be moving up the job ladder to these higher-paying brain jobs, whereas men are much more likely to just be moving from blue-collar jobs into not finding a job,” said Mr. Siu, who wrote the study with
Guido Matias Cortes
of the University of Manchester,
Nir Jaimovich
of Duke University and
Christopher J. Nekarda
of the Federal Reserve in Washington.
The changing demographics in the United States play a small role in the loss of midwage jobs, as do policies related to offshoring, unions and the minimum wage. But the study found that two-thirds of the decline in routine jobs is explained by a drop in the number of unemployed people who can get these jobs, and an increase in the number of people who had these jobs and lost them.

And the driver behind those shifts is technology.
“Over the very long run, technological progress is good for everybody, but over shorter time horizons, it’s not that everybody’s a winner,” Mr. Siu said. “Certain demographic groups like the young and less educated in another world would be doing fine, but in today’s world are not.”
The line between jobs that are considered routine and able to be done by a machine and those that require a human brain is a blurry one and becoming blurrier, said Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee of M.I.T., authors of “
The Second Machine Age
.”
“There are examples up and down the spectrum,” Mr. Brynjolfsson said. “It’s a process of scientific discovery. It’s not like we know exactly which task will be next to automate.”
Already, machines are learning to do certain jobs that once seemed confined to humans, from
elder care
to
wealth management
to
art
. The question is what will happen if these jobs also disappear.
